verses.en: “Indeed, my eyes have seen all this; my ears have heard and understood it.
verses.ja: 「見よ、私の目はこれらすべてを見、私の耳はそれを聞き、理解した。

verses.en: What you know, I know also; I am not inferior to you!
verses.ja: あなたがたの知っていることは、私もまた知っている。私はあなたがたに劣ってはいない！

verses.en: But I wish to speak to the Almighty, and I desire to argue my case with God.
verses.ja: しかし私は全能者に語ることを願い、神に対して自分の訴えを論じたいのだ。

verses.en: But you, however, are inventors of lies; all of you are worthless physicians!
verses.ja: だが、あなたがたは偽りを塗る者、あなたがたは皆、役立たずの医者だ！

verses.en: If only you would keep completely silent! For you, that would be wisdom.
verses.ja: どうか、完全に黙っていてくれればよいのに！ それこそがあなたがたの知恵となるだろう。

verses.en: Listen now to my argument, and be attentive to my lips’ contentions.
verses.ja: 今私の論議を聞き、私の唇の主張に注意を向けよ。

verses.en: Will you speak wickedly on God’s behalf? Will you speak deceitfully for him?
verses.ja: あなたがたは神のために不義を語るのか。神のために欺きを語るのか。

verses.en: Will you show him partiality? Will you argue the case for God?
verses.ja: あなたがたは神のえこひいきをするのか。神のために訴えを弁護するのか。

verses.en: Would it turn out well if he would examine you? Or as one deceives a man would you deceive him?
verses.ja: 神があなたがたを調べられるなら、うまくいくのだろうか。あるいは、人が人を欺くように、あなたがたは神を欺こうとするのか。

verses.en: He would certainly rebuke you if you secretly showed partiality.
verses.ja: もしあなたがたが密かにえこひいきをするなら、神は必ずやあなたがたを戒められる。

verses.en: Would not his splendor terrify you and the fear he inspires fall on you?
verses.ja: 神の威光はあなたがたを恐れさせ、神がもたらす恐怖はあなたがたに臨まないだろうか。

verses.en: Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.
verses.ja: あなたがたの格言は灰の箴言であり、あなたがたの防御は泥の防御である。

verses.en: “Refrain from talking with me so that I may speak; then let come to me what may.
verses.ja: 「私に語るのをやめよ。私が語るように。それから、何が起ころうとも私に臨ませよ。

verses.en: Why do I put myself in peril, and take my life in my hands?
verses.ja: なぜ私は自分の命を危険にさらし、自分の魂を手のうちに置くのだろうか。

verses.en: Even if he slays me, I will hope in him; I will surely defend my ways to his face.
verses.ja: たとえ神が私を殺されるとしても、私は神に望みを置く。私は自分の歩みを御前にしっかりと弁護する。

verses.en: Moreover, this will become my deliverance, for no godless person would come before him.
verses.ja: さらに、これが私の救いとなる。不敬虔な者は誰も御前に来ることがないからだ。

verses.en: Listen carefully to my words; let your ears be attentive to my explanation.
verses.ja: 私の言葉をよく聞き、私の説明にあなたがたの耳を傾けよ。

verses.en: See now, I have prepared my case; I know that I am right.
verses.ja: 見よ、私は自分の訴えを整えた。私は自分が正しいことを知っている。

verses.en: Who will contend with me? If anyone can, I will be silent and die.
verses.ja: 私と争う者は誰か。もし争える者がいるなら、私は黙して死のう。

verses.en: Only in two things spare me, O God, and then I will not hide from your face:
verses.ja: 神よ、ただ二つのことだけは私を免除してください。そうすれば、私はあなたの御顔から身を隠すことはありません。

verses.en: Remove your hand far from me and stop making me afraid with your terror.
verses.ja: あなたの手を遠く離し、あなたの恐怖によって私を脅かすのをやめてください。

verses.en: Then call, and I will answer, or I will speak, and you respond to me.
verses.ja: その上で呼びかけてください。私は答えましょう。あるいは私が語り、あなたが私に応答してください。

verses.en: How many are my iniquities and sins? Show me my transgression and my sin.
verses.ja: 私の咎と罪はいくつあるでしょうか。私の背きと罪を私に示してください。

verses.en: Why do you hide your face and regard me as your enemy?
verses.ja: なぜあなたは御顔を隠し、私を敵とみなされるのですか。

verses.en: Do you wish to torment a windblown leaf and chase after dry chaff?
verses.ja: あなたは風に吹き流される葉を責め苛み、乾いたもみがらを追い求められるのですか。

verses.en: For you write down bitter things against me and cause me to inherit the sins of my youth.
verses.ja: あなたは私に対する苦い事どもを書き記し、私の若き日の罪を受け継がせられる。

verses.en: And you put my feet in the stocks and you watch all my movements; you put marks on the soles of my feet.
verses.ja: あなたは私の足を足かせに入れ、私のすべての動きを見張り、私の足の裏に印をつけられる。

verses.en: So I waste away like something rotten, like a garment eaten by moths.
verses.ja: それゆえ私は、朽ちたもののようにおり、蛾に食われた衣のようになる。」

1.en: [解説]  Chapter  records Job’s charges against his friends for the way they used their knowledge (1-5), his warning that God would find out their insincerity (6-12), and his pleading of his cause to God in which he begs for God to remove his hand from him and that he would not terrify him with his majesty and that he would reveal the sins that caused such great suffering (13-28).
[翻訳注]  Hebrew has כֹּל (kol, “all”); there is no reason to add anything to the text to gain a meaning “all this.”

2.en: [翻訳注]  Heb “Like your knowledge”; in other words Job is saying that his knowledge is like their knowledge.
[翻訳注]  The pronoun makes the subject emphatic and stresses the contrast: “I know – I also.”
[翻訳注]  The verb “fall” is used here as it was in Job 4:13 to express becoming lower than someone, i.e., inferior.

3.en: [翻訳注]  The verb is simply the Piel imperfect אֲדַבֵּר (’adabber, “I speak”). It should be classified as a desiderative imperfect, saying, “I desire to speak.” This is reinforced with the verb “to wish, desire” in the second half of the verse.
[翻訳注]  The Hebrew title for God here is אֶל־שַׁדַּי (’el shadday, “El Shaddai”).
[翻訳注]  The infinitive absolute functions here as the direct object of the verb “desire” (see GKC 340 §113.b).
[翻訳注]  The infinitive הוֹכֵחַ (hokheakh) is from the verb יָכַח (yakhakh), which means “to argue, plead, debate.” It has the legal sense here of arguing a case (cf. 5:17).

4.en: [翻訳注]  The טֹפְלֵי־שָׁקֶר (tofÿle shaqer) are “plasterers of lies” (Ps 119:69). The verb means “to coat, smear, plaster.” The idea is that of imputing something that is not true. Job is saying that his friends are inventors of lies. The LXX was influenced by the next line and came up with “false physicians.”

[翻訳注]  The literal rendering of the construct would be “healers of worthlessness.” Ewald and Dillmann translated it “patchers” based on a meaning in Arabic and Ethiopic; this would give the idea “botchers.” But it makes equally good sense to take “healers” as the meaning, for Job’s friends came to minister comfort and restoration to him – but they failed. See P. Humbert, “Maladie et medicine dans l’AT,” RHPR 44 (1964): 1-29.

5.en: [翻訳注]  The construction is the imperfect verb in the wish formula preceded by the infinitive that intensifies it. The Hiphil is not directly causative here, but internally – “keep silent.”

[翻訳注]  The text literally reads, “and it would be for you for wisdom,” or “that it would become your wisdom.” Job is rather sarcastic here, indicating if they shut up they would prove themselves to be wise (see Prov 17:28).

6.en: [解説]  Job first will argue with his friends. His cause that he will plead with God begins in v. 13. The same root יָכַח (yakhakh, “argue, plead”) is used here as in v. 3b (see note). Synonymous parallelism between the two halves of this verse supports this translation.
[翻訳注]  The Hebrew word רִבוֹת (rivot, “disputes, contentions”) continues the imagery of presenting a legal case. The term is used of legal disputations and litigation. See, also, v. 19a.

7.en: [翻訳注]  The construction literally reads “speak iniquity.” The form functions adverbially. The noun עַוְלָה (’avlah) means “perversion; injustice; iniquity; falsehood.” Here it is parallel to רְמִיָּה (rÿmiyyah, “fraud; deceit; treachery”).
[翻訳注]  The expression “for God” means “in favor of God” or “on God’s behalf.” Job is amazed that they will say false things on God’s behalf.

8.en: [解説]  The idiom used here is “Will you lift up his face?” Here Job is being very sarcastic, for this expression usually means that a judge is taking a bribe. Job is accusing them of taking God’s side.
[翻訳注]  The same root is used here (רִיב, riv, “dispute, contention”) as in v. 6b (see note).

9.en: [翻訳注]  The verb חָפַר (khafar) means “to search out, investigate, examine.” In the conditional clause the imperfect verb expresses the hypothetical case.

[翻訳注]  Both the infinitive and the imperfect of תָּלַל (talal, “deceive, mock”) retain the ה (he) (GKC 148 §53.q). But for the alternate form, see F. C. Fensham, “The Stem HTL in Hebrew,” VT 9 (1959): 310-11. The infinitive is used here in an adverbial sense after the preposition.

10.en: [翻訳注]  The verbal idea is intensified with the infinitive absolute. This is the same verb used in v. 3; here it would have the sense of “rebuke, convict.”[解説]  Peake’s observation is worth noting, namely, that as Job attacks the unrighteousness of God boldly he nonetheless has confidence in God’s righteousness that would not allow liars to defend him.
[解説]  The use of the word “in secret” or “secretly” suggests that what they do is a guilty action (31:27a).

11.en: [解説]  The word translated “his majesty” or “his splendor” (שְׂאֵתוֹ, sÿ’eto) forms a play on the word “show partiality” (תִּשָּׂאוּן, tissa’un) in the last verse. They are both from the verb נָשַׂא (nasa’, “to lift up”).
[翻訳注]  On this verb in the Piel, see 7:14.
[翻訳注]  Heb “His dread”; the suffix is a subjective genitive.

12.en: [翻訳注]  The word is זִכְרֹנֵיכֶם (zikhronekhem, “your remembrances”). The word זִכָּרֹן (zikkaron) not only can mean the act of remembering, but also what is remembered – what provokes memory or is worth being remembered. In the plural it can mean all the memorabilia, and in this verse all the sayings and teachings. H. H. Rowley (Job [NCBC], 99) suggests that in Job’s speech it could mean “all your memorized sayings.”

[翻訳注]  The parallelism of “dust” and “ashes” is fairly frequent in scripture. But “proverbs of ashes” is difficult. The genitive is certainly describing the proverbs; it could be classified as a genitive of apposition, proverbs that are/have become ashes. Ashes represent something that at one time may have been useful, but now has been reduced to what is worthless.

[翻訳注]  There is a division of opinion on the source of this word. Some take it from “answer”, related to Arabic, Aramaic, and Syriac words for “answer,” and so translate it “responses” (JB). Others take it from a word for “back,” with a derived meaning of the “boss” of the shield, and translate it bulwark or “defenses” (NEB, RSV, NIV). The idea of “answers” may fit the parallelism better, but “defenses” can be taken figuratively to refer to verbal defenses.
[解説]  Any defense made with clay would crumble on impact.

13.en: [翻訳注]  The Hebrew has a pregnant construction: “be silent from me,” meaning “stand away from me in silence,” or “refrain from talking with me.” See GKC 384 §119.ff. The LXX omits “from me,” as do several commentators.

[翻訳注]  The verb is the Piel cohortative; following the imperative of the first colon this verb would show purpose or result. The inclusion of the independent personal pronoun makes the focus emphatic – “so that I (in my turn) may speak.”
[翻訳注]  The verb עָבַר (’avar, “pass over”) is used with the preposition עַל (’al, “upon”) to express the advent of misfortune, namely, something coming against him.
[翻訳注]  The interrogative pronoun מָה (mah) is used in indirect questions, here introducing a clause [with the verb understood] as the object – “whatever it be” (see GKC 443-44 §137.c).

14.en: [写本注]  Most editors reject עַל־מָה (’al mah) as dittography from the last verse.

[翻訳注]  Heb “why do I take my flesh in my teeth?” This expression occurs nowhere else. It seems to be drawn from animal imagery in which the wild beast seizes the prey and carries it off to a place of security. The idea would then be that Job may be destroying himself. An animal that fights with its flesh (prey) in its mouth risks losing it. Other commentators do not think this is satisfactory, but they are unable to suggest anything better.

15.en: [翻訳注]  There is a textual difficulty here that factors into the interpretation of the verse. The Kethib is לֹא (lo’, “not”), but the Qere is לוֹ (lo, “to him”). The RSV takes the former: “Behold, he will slay me, I have no hope.” The NIV takes it as “though he slay me, yet will I hope in him.” Job is looking ahead to death, which is not an evil thing to him. The point of the verse is that he is willing to challenge God at the risk of his life; and if God slays him, he is still confident that he will be vindicated – as he says later in this chapter. Other suggestions are not compelling. E. Dhorme (Job, 187) makes a slight change of אֲיַחֵל (’ayakhel, “I will hope”) to אַחִיל (’akhil, “I will [not] tremble”). A. B. Davidson (Job, 98) retains the MT, but interprets the verb more in line with its use in the book: “I will not wait” (cf. NLT).
[翻訳注]  On אַךְ (’akh, “surely”) see GKC 483 §153 on intensive clauses.

[翻訳注]  The verb once again is יָכָה (yakhah, in the Hiphil, “argue a case, plead, defend, contest”). But because the word usually means “accuse” rather than “defend,” I. L. Seeligmann proposed changing “my ways” to “his ways” (“Zur Terminologie für das Gerichtsverfahren im Wortschatz des biblischen Hebräisch,” VTSup 16 [1967]: 251-78). But the word can be interpreted appropriately in the context without emendation.

16.en: [解説]  The fact that Job will dare to come before God and make his case is evidence – to Job at least – that he is innocent.

17.en: [翻訳注]  The infinitive absolute intensifies the imperative, which serves here with the force of an immediate call to attention. In accordance with GKC 342 §113.n, the construction could be translated, “Keep listening” (so ESV).

[翻訳注]  The verb has to be supplied in this line, for the MT has “and my explanation in your ears.” In the verse, both “word” and “explanation” are Aramaisms (the latter appearing in Dan 5:12 for the explanation of riddles).

18.en: [翻訳注]  The particle הִנֵּה (hinneh) functions almost as an imperative here, calling attention to what follows: “look” (archaic: behold).
[翻訳注]  The verb עָרַךְ (’arakh) means “to set in order, set in array [as a battle], prepare” in the sense here of arrange and organize a lawsuit.
[翻訳注]  The pronoun is added because this is what the verse means.
[翻訳注]  The word מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat) usually means “judgment; decision.” Here it means “lawsuit” (and so a metonymy of effect gave rise to this usage; see Num 27:5; 2 Sam 15:4).

[翻訳注]  The pronoun is emphatic before the verb: “I know that it is I who am right.” The verb means “to be right; to be righteous.” Some have translated it “vindicated,” looking at the outcome of the suit.

19.en: [翻訳注]  The interrogative is joined with the emphatic pronoun, stressing “who is he [who] will contend,” or more emphatically, “who in the world will contend.” Job is confident that no one can bring charges against him. He is certain of success.
[解説]  Job is confident that he will be vindicated. But if someone were to show up and have proof of sin against him, he would be silent and die (literally “keep silent and expire”).

20.en: [翻訳注]  The line reads “do not do two things.”
[翻訳注]  “God” is supplied to the verse, for the address is now to him. Job wishes to enter into dispute with God, but he first appeals that God not take advantage of him with his awesome power.

21.en: [翻訳注]  The imperative הַרְחַק (harkhaq, “remove”; GKC 98 §29.q), from רָחַק (rakhaq, “far, be far”) means “take away [far away]; to remove.”

[解説]  This is a common, but bold, anthropomorphism. The fact that the word used is כַּף (kaf, properly “palm”) rather than יָד (yad, “hand,” with the sense of power) may stress Job’s feeling of being trapped or confined (see also Ps 139:5, 7).

22.en: [翻訳注]  The imperatives in the verse function like the future tense in view of their use for instruction or advice. The chiastic arrangement of the verb forms is interesting: imperative + imperfect, imperfect + imperative. The imperative is used for God, but the imperfect is used when Job is the subject. Job is calling for the court to convene – he will be either the defendant or the prosecutor.

23.en: [翻訳注]  The pronoun “my” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied here in the translation.

[解説]  Job uses three words for sin here: “iniquities,” which means going astray, erring; “sins,” which means missing the mark or the way; and “transgressions,” which are open rebellions. They all emphasize different kinds of sins and different degrees of willfulness. Job is demanding that any sins be brought up. Both Job and his friends agree that great afflictions would have to indicate great offenses – he wants to know what they are.

24.en: [解説]  The anthropomorphism of “hide the face” indicates a withdrawal of favor and an outpouring of wrath (see Ps 30:7 [8]; Isa 54:8; Ps 27:9). Sometimes God “hides his face” to make himself invisible or aloof (see 34:29). In either case, if God covers his face it is because he considers Job an enemy – at least this is what Job thinks.

25.en: [翻訳注]  The verb תַּעֲרוֹץ (ta’arots, “you torment”) is from עָרַץ (’arats), which usually means “fear; dread,” but can also mean “to make afraid; to terrify” (Isa 2:19,21). The imperfect is here taken as a desiderative imperfect: “why do you want to”; but it could also be a simple future: “will you torment.”

[翻訳注]  The word נִדָּף (niddaf) is “driven” from the root נָדַף (nadaf, “drive”). The words “by the wind” or the interpretation “windblown” has to be added for the clarification. Job is comparing himself to this leaf (so an implied comparison, called hypocatastasis) – so light and insubstantial that it is amazing that God should come after him. Guillaume suggests that the word is not from this root, but from a second root נָדַף (nadaf), cognate to Arabic nadifa, “to dry up” (A. Guillaume, “A Note on Isaiah 19:7,” JTS 14 [1963]: 382-83). But as D. J. A. Clines notes (Job [WBC], 283), a dried leaf is a driven leaf – a point Guillaume allows as he says there is ambiguity in the term.

[翻訳注]  The word קַשׁ (qash) means “chaff; stubble,” or a wisp of straw. It is found in Job 41:20-21 for that which is so worthless and insignificant that it is hardly worth mentioning. If dried up or withered, it too will be blown away in the wind.

26.en: [翻訳注]  The meaning is that of writing down a formal charge against someone (cf. Job 31:15).
[解説]  Job acknowledges sins in his youth, but they are trifling compared to the suffering he now endures. Job thinks it unjust of God to persecute him now for those – if that is what is happening.

27.en: [翻訳注]  The word occurs here and in Job 33:11. It could be taken as “stocks,” in which the feet were held fast; or it could be “shackles,” which allowed the prisoner to move about. The parallelism favors the latter, if the two lines are meant to be referring to the same thing.
[翻訳注]  The word means “ways; roads; paths,” but it is used here in the sense of the “way” in which one goes about his activities.

[翻訳注]  The verb תִּתְחַקֶּה (titkhaqqeh) is a Hitpael from the root חָקָה (khaqah, parallel to חָקַק, khaqaq). The word means “to engrave” or “to carve out.” This Hitpael would mean “to imprint something on oneself” (E. Dhorme [Job, 192] says on one’s mind, and so derives the meaning “examine.”). The object of this is the expression “on the roots of my feet,” which would refer to where the feet hit the ground. Since the passage has more to do with God’s restricting Job’s movement, the translation “you set a boundary to the soles of my feet” would be better than Dhorme’s view. The image of inscribing or putting marks on the feet is not found elsewhere. It may be, as Pope suggests, a reference to marking the slaves to make tracking them easier. The LXX has “you have penetrated to my heels.”

28.en: [翻訳注]  Heb “and he.” Some of the commentators move the verse and put it after Job 14:2, 3 or 6.

[翻訳注]  The word רָקָב (raqav) is used elsewhere in the Bible of dry rot in a house, or rotting bones in a grave. It is used in parallelism with “moth” both here and in Hos 5:12. The LXX has “like a wineskin.” This would be from רֹקֶב (roqev, “wineskin”). This word does not occur in the Hebrew Bible, but is attested in Sir 43:20 and in Aramaic. The change is not necessary.
